claim: The brain is capable of large-scale reorganization in blindness or after massive injury.
source: The brain is capable of large-scale reorganization in blindness or after massive injury.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws on established scientific knowledge about brain plasticity in sensory deprivation or injury contexts.

claim: Large-scale reorganization crosses the division into separate sensory cortices (visual, somatosensory...).
source: Such reorganization crosses the division into separate sensory cortices (visual, somatosensory...).
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about cross-modal plasticity in sensory deprivation.

claim: The visual cortex of the blind becomes active during tactile Braille reading.
source: As its result, the visual cortex of the blind becomes active during tactile Braille reading.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research in the introduction section.

claim: Sighted adults who learned Braille showed enhanced activity for tactile reading in the visual cortex.
source: Subjects showed enhanced activity for tactile reading in the visual cortex, including the visual word form area (VWFA) that was modulated by their Braille reading speed and strengthened resting-state connectivity between visual and somatosensory cortices.
evidence: This claim is supported by the fMRI data presented in the study, as shown in Figures 1D-G and described in the results section.

claim: Enhanced activity for tactile reading in sighted adults included the visual word form area (VWFA).
source: Subjects showed enhanced activity for tactile reading in the visual cortex, including the visual word form area (VWFA)
evidence: This is directly supported by fMRI data showing VWFA activation during tactile Braille reading.

claim: VWFA activity during tactile reading was modulated by Braille reading speed.
source: Subjects showed enhanced activity for tactile reading in the visual cortex, including the visual word form area (VWFA) that was modulated by their Braille reading speed
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis showing correlation between reading speed and VWFA activation (Figure 1G).

claim: Learning Braille strengthened resting-state connectivity between visual and somatosensory cortices.
source: strengthened resting-state connectivity between visual and somatosensory cortices.
evidence: This is supported by resting-state fMRI data showing increased functional connectivity (Figure 3).

claim: TMS disruption of VWFA activity decreased tactile reading accuracy.
source: Moreover, TMS disruption of VWFA activity decreased their tactile reading accuracy.
evidence: This is supported by the TMS experiment data showing decreased accuracy when VWFA was stimulated (Figure 4B).

claim: Large-scale reorganization is a viable mechanism recruited when learning complex skills.
source: Our results indicate that large-scale reorganization is a viable mechanism recruited when learning complex skills.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing cross-modal plasticity in sighted adults learning Braille.

claim: Experience-driven plasticity in the adult brain is thought to operate within the limits of sensory divisions.
source: At the systems level, experience-driven plasticity is thought to operate within the limits of sensory divisions, where the visual cortex processes visual stimuli and responds to visual training, the tactile cortex processes tactile stimuli and responds to tactile training, and so on.
evidence: This represents the current view in the field, based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Departure from sensory division constraints is usually reported only during large-scale reorganization induced by sensory loss or injury.
source: A departure from this rule is usually reported only during large-scale reorganization induced by sensory loss or injury (Hirsch et al., 2015; Lomber et al., 2011; Merabet and Pascual-Leone, 2010; Pavani and Roder, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The ventral visual cortex is activated in blind subjects who read Braille.
source: The ventral visual cortex, in particular, is activated in blind subjects who read Braille (Büchel et al., 1998; Reich et al., 2011; Sadato et al., 2002, 1996)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Lesions of the ventral visual cortex impair Braille reading in blind subjects.
source: and lesions of this area impair Braille reading (Hamilton et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The visual cortex has the innate connectivity required to carry out reading in a modality different than vision.
source: This visual cortex thus has the innate connectivity required to carry out a complex perceptual task – reading – in a modality different than vision.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that blind subjects can read Braille using visual cortex.

claim: It is unclear to what extent the connectivity for cross-modal processing is preserved and functional in the normal, adult brain.
source: It is unclear, however, to what extent this connectivity is preserved and functional in the normal, adult brain.
evidence: This represents a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Some form of cross-modal recruitment of the visual cortex could be possible in normal healthy adults.
source: A growing amount of evidence suggests that some form of cross-modal recruitment of the visual cortex could be possible in the normal healthy adults (Amedi et al., 2007; Kim and Zatorre, 2011; Powers et al., 2012; Saito et al., 2006; Zangenehpour and Zatorre, 2010; Merabet et al., 2004; Zangaladze et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The behavioural relevance of cross-modal cortical mechanisms in normal adults remains unclear, especially for complex stimuli.
source: Nonetheless, the behavioural relevance of these cortical mechanisms remains unclear, especially for complex stimuli.
evidence: This represents a limitation in previous research that the current study addresses.

claim: Several experiments failed to find cross-modal reorganization in sighted subjects, even after extensive training.
source: Notably, several experiments failed to find such cross-modal reorganization in sighted subjects, even after extensive training (Kupers et al., 2006; Ptito et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cross-modal plastic changes in subjects blindfolded for several days quickly vanished once the subjects removed their blindfolds.
source: One study found cross-modal plastic changes in subjects that were blindfolded for several days (Merabet et al., 2008), but these plastic changes quickly vanished once the subjects removed their blindfolds.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Twenty-nine sighted adults took part in the study.
source: Twenty-nine sighted adults, Braille teachers and professionals, students specializing in the education of the blind, and family members of blind people, took part in the study.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study participants.

claim: All subjects were naive in tactile Braille reading at the start of the study.
source: All of them were naive in tactile Braille reading (Appendix 1.1).
evidence: This is a statement about the baseline characteristics of the study participants.

claim: All participants completed an intensive, tailor-made, 9-month-long tactile Braille reading course.
source: All the participants completed an intensive, tailor-made, 9-month-long tactile Braille reading course (Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the intervention used in the study.

claim: The majority of subjects progressed significantly in tactile reading, reaching an average performance of 6.20 words per minute.
source: The majority progressed significantly in tactile reading, reaching an average performance of 6.20 words per minute read aloud (WPM) (SD=3.94, range = 0–17, Appendix 1.1) at the end of the course.
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral data from the study.

claim: Subjects improved in reading Braille characters visually after the course.
source: Because the course curriculum included learning to recognize Braille letters by sight, the subjects also improved in reading Braille characters visually (Appendix 1.2).
evidence: This is a report of behavioral data from the study.

claim: After the course, tactile Braille reading evoked activations in the visual word form area (VWFA) compared to the tactile control.
source: Compared to the tactile control, tactile reading after the course evoked activations in the visual word form area (VWFA), the lateral occipital area and other areas (Tables 1–3).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data shown in Figure 1D and Tables 1-3.

claim: Whole-brain fMRI analysis showed that after the course, activation to tactile Braille reading relative to the tactile control condition peaked within the Visual Word Form Area (VWFA) at MNI = -45 -58 -12, Z = 5.18.
source: Whole-brain fMRI analysis showed that after the course, activation to tactile Braille reading relative to the tactile control condition peaked within the Visual Word Form Area (VWFA), (Figure 1D, peak MNI = -45 -58 -12, Z = 5.18)
evidence: This is a direct report of fMRI data analysis results.

claim: The VWFA is a ventral visual stream region known to be involved in visual reading.
source: a ventral visual stream (Van Essen, 2005) region known to be involved in visual reading (Dehaene and Cohen, 2011; Price and Devlin, 2011; Szwed et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Additional activations for tactile Braille reading were observed in the intraparietal sulcus, supramarginal gyrus, and frontal areas.
source: Additional activations were observed in the intraparietal sulcus, supramarginal gyrus, and frontal areas (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data reported in Table 1.

claim: The increase in VWFA activation after the course was specific for tactile reading.
source: The latter confirmed that the increase in visual cortex activation after the course was specific for tactile reading.
evidence: This is supported by the interaction analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The only significant whole-brain correlate with tactile reading proficiency was found in the ventral visual system.
source: When we modeled the modulation of fMRI responses to tactile Braille by the subjects' reading speed, the only significant whole-brain correlate with tactile reading proficiency was found in the ventral visual system (k=103 voxels).
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: No increase in activation to visual words was found following the course.
source: Indeed, we found no increase in activation to visual words following the course.
evidence: This is a direct report of fMRI analysis results.

claim: The only increases in activation to visual Braille were found in the default mode network nodes in the parietal and prefrontal cortices.
source: The only increases in activation to visual Braille were found in the default mode network nodes in the parietal and prefrontal cortices (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C, Table 2, Appendix 1.3).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and Table 2.

claim: The whole-brain ANOVA did not reveal any activation in the primary and secondary somatosensory cortices, even at an exploratory threshold of p=0.01 voxel-wise.
source: Importantly, the analyses mentioned in this section (Figure 1D–F), including the whole-brain ANOVA, did not reveal any activation in the primary and secondary somatosensory cortices, even at an exploratory threshold of p=0.01 voxel-wise.
evidence: This is a direct report of fMRI analysis results.

claim: Regression analysis revealed one significant cluster modulated by tactile reading speed, located in the left inferior occipital gyrus at MNI = -45 -76 -12, Z = 3.69.
source: This regression analysis revealed one significant cluster, located in the left inferior occipital gyrus (Figure 1G; MNI = -45 -76 -12, Z = 3.69, Table 3).
evidence: This is a direct report of regression analysis results.

claim: Single letter recognition speed correlated with tactile Braille activations, supporting the significance of the visual cortex in learning to read Braille.
source: A similar result was obtained when we correlated single letter recognition speed with tactile Braille activations, which further supports the significance of the visual cortex in learning to read Braille (Table 3, Appendix 1.4).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis reported in Table 3.

claim: No correlations were found for other reading speed measures or imagery activations.
source: We found no such correlations for other reading speed measures (e.g. visual Braille reading speed) or imagery activations (e.g. imagining tactile Braille; see Appendix 1.5).
evidence: This is a direct report of analysis results.

claim: The ventral visual activations for tactile reading cannot be explained as a by-product of imagery.
source: These observations indicate that the ventral visual activations for tactile reading cannot be explained as a by-product of imagery.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of correlation between imagery activations and reading performance.

claim: The two Braille conditions (visual and tactile) had the most similar activation patterns in the VWFA (r=0.48).
source: Using MVPA-RSA ('Materials and methods'), we found that the two Braille conditions (visual and tactile) had the most similar activation patterns in the VWFA (Figure 2A,r=0.48)
evidence: This is supported by representational similarity analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The correlations of the two Braille conditions with visual words were much weaker than the correlation between the two Braille conditions.
source: The correlations of the two Braille conditions with visual words were much weaker (Figure 2A, 'Materials and methods' and Appendix 1.6).
evidence: This is supported by representational similarity analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The neural representations of the two versions of Braille script were partially similar and distinct from the well-established representation for visual words.
source: Despite a difference in modality (visual vs. tactile), the neural representations of the two versions of Braille script were partially similar and distinct from the well-established representation for visual words.
evidence: This is an inference based on the representational similarity analysis results.

claim: In the VWFA, the response to tactile Braille words changed from a de-activation to a positive activation following the Braille course.
source: In the VWFA (Figure 2B; all ROIs are in the left hemisphere) following the Braille course, the response to tactile Braille words changed from de-activation to positive activation, resulting in a significant difference between tactile words and their control (interaction: F(1,28)=18.5; p<001).
evidence: This is supported by ROI analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The VWFA showed strong responses to visual Braille words, similar to previously reported responses to novel visual alphabets.
source: The VWFA also showed strong responses to visual Braille words, similar to previously reported responses to novel visual alphabets (e.g. Szwed et al., 2014; Vogel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by ROI analysis data and citations to previous research.

claim: VWFA responses to visual Braille words remained unchanged throughout the course.
source: These responses remained unchanged throughout the course.
evidence: This is a direct report of ROI analysis results.

claim: The lateral occipital area showed a similar emergence of responses to tactile Braille words after the course as the VWFA.
source: The lateral occipital area (Figure 2C) showed a similar emergence of responses to tactile Braille words after the course as well.
evidence: This is supported by ROI analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There was no significant change in primary somatosensory cortex activation to tactile Braille words and no after-course differences between tactile Braille words and the tactile control.
source: In the current study, however, there was no significant change in activation to tactile Braille words and no after-course differences between tactile Braille words and the tactile control (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a direct report of ROI analysis results.

claim: In the secondary somatosensory cortex, there was only a non-specific drop in activation to all tactile stimuli (F(1,28)=7.62, p=0.01), with no difference between tactile Braille words and the tactile control after the course.
source: In the secondary somatosensory cortex (MNI: -51 -25 15), we found only a non-specific drop in activation to all tactile stimuli (F(1,28)=7.62, p=0.01), with no difference between tactile Braille words and the tactile control after the course.
evidence: This is a direct report of ROI analysis results.

claim: A drop in activation for the control condition was observed in the intraparietal sulcus (t(28)=2.76, p=0.01).
source: A drop in activation for the control condition was observed in the posterior attentional network (intraparietal sulcus, IPS, Figure 2E, t(28)=2.76, p=0.01).
evidence: This is a direct report of ROI analysis results.

claim: The Braille reading course led to an increase in activation to tactile Braille words in visual areas but not in the somatosensory cortex.
source: Thus, the Braille reading course led to an increase in activation to tactile Braille words in visual areas but not in the somatosensory cortex.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the ROI analysis results.

claim: Following the course, there was an increase in resting-state functional connectivity between the VWFA seed and the left primary somatosensory cortex (p<0.001, corrected; Z=4.57; MNI: -57 -24 45).
source: Following the course, we observed an increase in resting-state functional connectivity between the VWFA seed and the left primary somatosensory cortex (Figure 3A, red; p<0.001, corrected for multiple comparisons; Z=4.57; MNI: -57 -24 45; 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is supported by resting-state fMRI analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The increase in VWFA-S1 functional connectivity was the only statistically significant positive effect found in resting-state analysis.
source: This increase was the only statistically significant positive effect found.
evidence: This is a direct report of resting-state fMRI analysis results.

claim: After the course, the VWFA showed decreased functional connectivity with other visual areas, bilaterally.
source: The same comparison showed a decrease in the VWFA's functional connectivity with other visual areas, bilaterally.
evidence: This is a direct report of resting-state fMRI analysis results.

claim: After the course, the VWFA-S1 functional connectivity level was correlated with the subjects' progress in tactile Braille reading speed (r(27)=0.49, p=0.007).
source: Furthermore, after the course, the VWFA-S1 functional connectivity level was correlated with the subjects' progress in tactile Braille reading speed (in the month preceding the after-course scan, Figure 3; r(27)=0.49, p=0.007).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The VWFA increased its coupling with the somatosensory cortex while decreasing its coupling with other visual areas.
source: The VWFA thus increased its coupling with the somatosensory cortex while decreasing its coupling with other visual areas.
evidence: This is a summary of the resting-state fMRI findings.

claim: VWFA-S1 functional connectivity was behaviorally relevant for tactile reading.
source: This VWFA-S1 functional connectivity was behaviorally relevant for tactile reading
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between connectivity and reading performance.

claim: VWFA-S1 functional connectivity was likely to be dynamically modulated in a relatively short learning period.
source: and was likely to be dynamically modulated in a relatively short learning period (similar to: Lewis et al., 2009)
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation with recent progress and citation to previous research.

claim: TMS to the VWFA decreased the accuracy of reading Braille words (t(8)=3.02, p=0.016).
source: As predicted, TMS to the VWFA decreased the accuracy of reading Braille words (t(8)=3.02, p=0.016, Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by TMS experiment data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The VWFA is necessary for reading tactile Braille words.
source: This TMS result shows that the VWFA is necessary for reading tactile Braille words.
evidence: This is an inference based on the TMS disruption results.

claim: TMS effects on control stimuli (Braille pseudowords) and control sites (lateral occipital area, vertex) were not significant.
source: We also tested for effects of TMS on control stimuli (Braille pseudowords) and control sites (lateral occipital area, vertex) (Figure 4B) and none of these tests resulted in significant effects (VWFA, Braille pseudowords: t(8)=0.03, p=0.977; lateral occipital area, Braille words: t(8)=0.18, p=0.859; lateral occipital area, Braille pseudowords: t(8)=0.03, p=0.979; vertex, Braille words: t(8)=1.26, p=0.243; vertex, Braille pseudowords: t(8)=0.02, p=0.986).
evidence: This is a direct report of TMS experiment results.

claim: The TMS experiment was underpowered to statistically verify the specificity of the TMS effect.
source: However, given the small number of subjects in this part of our study, our TMS experiment was underpowered to statistically verify the specificity of the TMS effect
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in the study design.

claim: The occipitotemporal visual cortex (VWFA, MNI y≈-60) can represent stimuli in a modality other than vision.
source: Our results demonstrate that the occipitotemporal visual cortex (VWFA, MNI y≈-60) can represent stimuli in a modality other than vision.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined fMRI and TMS results.

claim: TMS to the VWFA can disrupt tactile reading, demonstrating the importance of this representation for sensory processing.
source: The fact that TMS to the VWFA can disrupt tactile reading demonstrates the importance of this representation for sensory processing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the TMS results.

claim: TMS applied to the lateral occipital area (LOA) did not disturb tactile reading process.
source: However, TMS applied to LOA did not disturb tactile reading process (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a direct report of TMS experiment results.

claim: The lateral occipital area is activated in various visual word recognition tasks.
source: While the LOA is activated in various visual word recognition tasks (Duncan et al., 2009; Wright et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Lesions of the lateral occipital area do not affect reading itself.
source: its lesions seems not to affect reading itself (Cavina-Pratesi et al., 2015; Milner et al., 1991; Philipose et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Visual and tactile reading share similar neural correlates along the ventral visual stream.
source: The increase of activity in both LOA and VWFA for tactile reading thus suggest that visual and tactile reading share similar neural correlates along the ventral visual stream.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of activations observed.

claim: The exact function of the lateral occipital area in reading is more accessory than critical.
source: However, the exact function of LOA in reading seems to be more accessory than critical.
evidence: This is an inference based on the TMS results and previous literature.

claim: The ventral visual cortex was activated when subjects heard auditory words and then imagined reading them in tactile Braille.
source: The ventral visual cortex was also activated when subjects heard auditory words and then imagined reading them in tactile Braille (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI data from the control imagery experiment.

claim: Robust object activations were observed in the ventral visual stream during the object imagery task (left: MNI -45 -67 -9, Z=6.68, right: MNI 45 -67 -5, Z=5.94).
source: We also observed robust object activations in the object imagery task (ventral visual stream, left: MNI -45 -67 -9, Z=6.68, right: MNI 45 -67 -5, Z=5.94)
evidence: This is a direct report of fMRI data from the control imagery experiment.

claim: The object activations confirm that subjects successfully engaged in imagery during the experiment.
source: which confirms that subjects successfully engaged in imagery during the experiment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of expected activations during imagery tasks.

claim: Visual cortex activations for tactile reading cannot be explained as a by-product of visual imagery.
source: Thus, visual cortex activations for tactile reading cannot be explained as a by-product of visual imagery.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple lines of evidence including TMS results and lack of correlation with imagery measures.

claim: Visual cortex activations for tactile reading constitute the signature of a new, tactile script representation emerging in the visual cortex.
source: Instead, they constitute the signature of a new, tactile script representation emerging in the visual cortex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of results showing functional visual cortex activation for tactile reading.

claim: Cortical reorganization that crosses sensory boundaries is prominent in blind and deaf humans.
source: Cortical reorganization that crosses the sensory boundaries is prominent in blind and deaf humans (Hirsch et al., 2015; Pavani and Roder, 2012; Sadato et al., 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Cortical reorganization that crosses sensory boundaries is prominent in congenitally deaf cats.
source: and in congenitally deaf cats (Lomber et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In congenitally deaf cats, the deprived auditory areas play a vital role in the deaf cats' superior visual perception.
source: In the latter, the deprived auditory areas play a vital role in the deaf cats' superior visual perception.
evidence: This claim is based on the cited research on deaf cats.

claim: Previous studies using the same paradigms in non-deprived humans and cats did not find any signs of cross-modal reorganization.
source: The above-mentioned studies used the same paradigms in non-deprived humans and cats, but did not find any signs of cross-modal reorganization (e.g. Figure 7 in Sadato et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Tactile training leads to changes in somatosensory activation to tactile stimuli.
source: This result might seem incompatible with a large body of data showing that tactile training leads to changes in somatosensory activation to tactile stimuli (Guic et al., 2008; Kupers et al., 2006; Pleger et al., 2003; Ptito et al., 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Previous experiments showing somatosensory changes used simple stimuli and short learning periods.
source: However, all the above-mentioned experiments used simple stimuli, such as gratings, and short learning periods.
evidence: This is a characterization of previous research based on the cited studies.

claim: The current experiment was longer (9 months) and used complex stimuli - entire Braille words.
source: Our experiment was longer (9 months) and used complex stimuli - entire Braille words.
evidence: This is a direct description of the study design.

claim: At the initial stage of Braille learning, the somatosensory cortex might have increased its response to Braille words.
source: Experiments that study learning-related plasticity at multiple time points (Lövdén et al., 2013) suggest that at the initial stage of Braille learning, the somatosensory cortex might have increased its response to Braille words.
evidence: This is speculation based on previous research about learning-related plasticity.

claim: As the effects of early sensory learning consolidated in the somatosensory cortex, the cortical focus of learning shifted to the ventral visual stream.
source: Then, as the effects of early sensory learning consolidated in the somatosensory cortex, the cortical focus of learning shifted elsewhere, in our case the ventral visual stream.
evidence: This is speculation about the temporal dynamics of plasticity based on the observed results.

claim: Previous studies have suggested that cross-modal plasticity is possible mainly as a result of massive sensory deprivation or injury.
source: Previous studies (Büchel et al., 1998; Lomber et al., 2011; Merabet and Pascual-Leone, 2010; Sadato et al., 2002, 1996) have suggested that cross-modal plasticity is possible mainly as a result of massive sensory deprivation or injury.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Given a long training period and a complex task, the normal brain is capable of large-scale plasticity that overcomes the division into separate sensory cortices.
source: Our results demonstrate that given a long training period and a complex task, the normal brain is capable of large-scale plasticity that overcomes the division into separate sensory cortices.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study results.

claim: The exact mechanisms of cross-modal plasticity might be different in deprived and non-deprived subjects.
source: The exact mechanisms of this plasticity might of course be different in deprived and non-deprived subjects.
evidence: This is speculation about potential differences in mechanisms.

claim: Professional pianists activate their auditory cortex when viewing mute video recordings of a piano key being pressed.
source: Professional pianists, for example, were shown to activate their auditory cortex when viewing mute video recordings of a piano key being pressed (Haslinger et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The behavioral relevance of cross-modal activations in normal adults was previously demonstrated only for simple tactile stimuli: grating orientation and distance judgment.
source: The behavioral relevance of such activations, however, was demonstrated only for simple tactile stimuli: grating orientation (Zangaladze et al., 1999) and distance judgment (Merabet et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Large-scale plasticity is a viable mechanism recruited when learning complex skills.
source: Its results suggest that large-scale plasticity is a viable mechanism recruited when learning complex skills.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study results.

claim: The morphology of cerebral cortex is substantially less genetically heritable in humans than in chimpanzees.
source: This conclusion is congruent with a recent comparative study showing that the morphology of cerebral cortex is substantially less genetically heritable in humans than in chimpanzees (Gomez-Robles et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Relaxed genetic control of cortex morphology might be the reason for homo sapiens' increased learning abilities and greater behavioral flexibility.
source: Such relaxed genetic control might be the reason for homo sapiens' increased learning abilities and greater behavioral flexibility.
evidence: This is speculation based on the cited comparative study.

claim: The dominant view describes brain plasticity as necessarily constrained by sensory boundaries.
source: Despite evidence for cross-modal plasticity of the human brain, the dominant view still describes it as necessarily constrained by the sensory boundaries (e.g. Figure 18–2 in: Kandel et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a textbook.

claim: The study provides clear-cut evidence that learning-related neuroplasticity can overcome the sensory division.
source: Our study provides a clear-cut evidence that learning-related neuroplasticity can overcome the sensory division.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study results.

claim: The findings call for a re-assessment of our view of the functional organization of the brain.
source: This calls for a re-assessment of our view of the functional organization of the brain.
evidence: This is an implication drawn from the study's conclusions.

claim: Thirty-six subjects took part in the first fMRI study (32 females, 4 males; mean age = 29.17).
source: Thirty-six subjects took part in the first fMRI study (32 females, 4 males; mean age = 29.17).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study participants.

claim: All subjects were right-handed, fluent in Polish and had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
source: All were right-handed, fluent in Polish and had normal or corrected-to-normal vision.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the characteristics of study participants.

claim: All but three subjects were familiar with Braille visually.
source: All but three subjects were familiar with Braille visually (see Appendix 1.2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the baseline characteristics of participants.

claim: During the first fMRI examination, one subject was eliminated from the study due to a medical condition.
source: During the first fMRI examination, one subject was eliminated from the study due to a medical condition discovered by the neurologist supervising the study.
evidence: This is a direct statement about subject attrition.

claim: Two subjects resigned right after the first session for personal reasons.
source: Right after the first session, two subjects resigned for personal reasons.
evidence: This is a direct statement about subject attrition.

claim: Four subjects resigned during the tactile Braille reading course.
source: Another four subjects resigned during the tactile Braille reading course.
evidence: This is a direct statement about subject attrition.

claim: Nine subjects who achieved tactile reading speeds between 3 to 17 WPM participated in the TMS experiment.
source: At the end of the course, nine of the subjects mentioned above who achieved tactile reading speeds between 3 to 17 WPM participated in the TMS experiment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the TMS experiment participants.

claim: The tactile Braille course was based on individual exercises, to be performed while blindfolded.
source: Briefly, the course was based on individual exercises, to be performed while blindfolded.
evidence: This is a direct description of the intervention method.

claim: Subjects were instructed to train on one A4 sheet every day (approximately 20 min).
source: Subjects were instructed to train on one A4 sheet every day (approximately 20 min).
evidence: This is a direct description of the training protocol.

claim: The subjects' progress was monitored by qualified Braille teachers during monthly meetings.
source: The subjects' progress was monitored by qualified Braille teachers during monthly meetings.
evidence: This is a direct description of the study procedures.

claim: In the second half of the course, subjects were encouraged to focus mainly on whole-word reading.
